characters: Akrofi: a curious nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a teal-and-khaki primary uniform shirt and khaki shorts, with a notebook and pencil.
Lekettey: his friendly nine-year-old classmate in a matching uniform shirt, wearing a simple black wristwatch.
Madam Salamatu: their encouraging science teacher in an emerald-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A curious voice for Akrofi; a patient, clear teacher voice for Madam Salamatu; a friendly voice for Lekettey
narrationPlan.pace: Thoughtful and clear, with a pause at each step (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, curious tune with a ticking clock (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Everyday materials such as sugar, salt, spoons, and clear cups make fair-test investigations practical in any Ghanaian classroom.
Safety rule: pupils use safe warm tap water or sun-warmed water; boiling or very hot water is handled only by adults.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the science: equal amounts of sugar with equal stirring dissolve faster in warmer water than in colder water.
Verify that the safety reminder restricting hot water to adults is prominent.

teacherGuide.overview: An inquiry-science story introducing controlled (“fair”) testing and repeatability, while showing learners that an imperfect first try is a valuable step in scientific thinking.
learningGoals: Explain why changing three things at once makes a test unfair.
Identify the one variable changed and the variables kept the same.
Carry out and repeat a safe dissolving test using warm and cold tap water.
beforeReading: Ask: if two runners start at different places, is the race fair? Connect that idea to a science test.
whileReading: Pause after page 2 and let learners spot all three mistakes in Akrofi’s first test before turning to page 3.
afterReading: Run the two-cup sugar test in groups using safe warm tap water and cool water.
Complete the sentence frame: “We changed ___. We kept ___ and ___ the same.”
discussion: Why was Akrofi’s first mistake actually helpful?
Why do scientists test three times instead of stopping after one try?
reflection: Tell about a time when a mistake helped you do something better on your second try.

mathsExtension.task: Akrofi repeated the two-cup test 3 times, using 1 level spoon of sugar per cup each time. How many level spoons of sugar did he use in all?
If the warm cup dissolved sugar in 25 seconds and the cold cup took 45 seconds (suppose), how many seconds faster was the warm cup?

support: Provide a three-box planning card: Change ONE thing / Keep the SAME / Measure.
stretch: Design a fair test to find out whether fine salt or coarse salt dissolves faster in room-temperature water.

culturalNotes: Everyday materials such as sugar, salt, spoons, and clear cups make fair-test investigations practical in any Ghanaian classroom.
Safety rule: pupils use safe warm tap water or sun-warmed water; boiling or very hot water is handled only by adults.
localiseThis: Use granulated sugar or salt and clear reusable plastic cups.
Never allow pupils to pour or carry boiling water; use warm tap or sun-warmed water only.

factCheck.claim: Sugar dissolves faster in warm water than in cold water when all other variables are kept constant.
factCheck.explanation: Higher water temperature increases molecular motion and collision frequency, speeding up the rate of dissolving in a controlled fair test.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Ghana Upper Primary Integrated Science Curriculum (Mixtures, Dissolving, and Fair Testing)
